newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Savings banks urge legislation break ahead of EMU.
newsitem.headline: Savings banks urge legislation break ahead of EMU.

text.p: Savings banks called on the European Commission on Friday for a legislation break on such areas as consumer policy as they struggle to get ready for the European single currency.

The banks, which weight 1.6 trillion European currency units ($1.8 trillion) in deposits in Europe or about 25 percent of total banking deposits, said the change to the Euro -- as the new currency will be called -- was a complex and expensive process and new regulatory initiatives would add to the burden.

"We demand a moratorium as regards new EU legislation during the preparation period for the single currency, so that efforts can be concentrated on this major issue," the European Savings Banks Group (ESBG) told a news conference.

Because their customer base is made essentially of small depositors and small and medium-sized businesses, the savings banks argue that they have proportionally higher costs in informing and preparing for the adoption of the Euro than commercial banks.

This comes on top of huge costs involved in changing the banks' technology for the Euro and to cope with the so-called "millenium bug" affecting computers because of the fact that software systems use a two-digit format to show the year.

It is usually considered that the technical changes for the Euro will not necessarily represent an additional spending for banks since they will have to adapt their computer systems to enter the year 2000. But ESBG's director for legal affairs, Adriana Alvarez, disagreed.
"One starts to see it might not be possible to incorporate the costs into the millenium costs," she said.
Alvarez added that the Euro costs will be higher than foreseen only one or two years ago.
The estimates by the Spanish banking sector as a whole range from 610 million Ecus to 1.8 million Ecus, the ESBG said, adding that its own assessment of the costs would be ready soon.
The European Banking Federation in 1995 estimated the costs for the entire sector at between 8.0 to 10 billion Ecus.

The Euro will in principle be created in January 1, 1999 in the EU countries found to meet strict economic criteria on sound finance, inflation and currency stability. But the coins and notes will not reach people's pockets before another two years.

The savings banks, which like their commercial rivals have to put up with recently imposed rules aimed at making small cross-border payment transfers cheaper and quicker, argue that there should be no other "unnecessary regulations" to avoid disturbing the changeover to the Euro.

This was a reference, in particular, to a European Commission plan to regulate distance selling and other measures to ensure consumers, not only firms including banks, get their fair share of the 15-nation border-free market.
The only exception in ESBG's call for less legislation concerned the fiscal area where different national tax laws were harming fair competition.
